The old days

What TDD is, and why it works for humans

The old days

TDD myths

“TDD is about testing”

“TDD is writing the tests first”

“You don’t write ‘the tests’ first. You write a test first.”

Tim Ottinger

“TDD is not really about writing tests before code. It’s about using tests in short-lived RGR cycles as a tool to design code.”

Andrea Laforgia

“The tests that drive our design often correspond to good regression tests, but certainly not always.”

Jason Gorman

The screenshots are the original LinkedIn posts: people who teach TDD keep having to write about these misconceptions. All three come back later. Ottinger returns on the tiny-steps slide (GLM wrote all its tests up front). Laforgia returns on the charade slide (by his definition the agents did test-first, not TDD). Gorman returns on tiny steps and in mutation testing; he mutation-tests new code routinely.

The old days

Gold plating

46

lines of code with strategy, abstract factory and singleton patterns!

interface MessageStrategy {
  public void sendMessage();
}
abstract class AbstractStrategyFactory {
  public abstract MessageStrategy createStrategy(MessageBody mb);
}
class MessageBody {
  Object payload;
  public Object getPayload() {
    return payload;
  }
  public void configure(Object obj) {
    payload = obj;
  }
  public void send(MessageStrategy ms) {
    ms.sendMessage();
  }
}
public class MyProgram {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    MessageBody mb = new MessageBody();
    mb.configure("Hello World!");
    AbstractStrategyFactory asf = DefaultFactory.getInstance();

    MessageStrategy strategy = asf.createStrategy(mb);
    mb.send(strategy);
  }
}
class DefaultFactory extends AbstractStrategyFactory {
  private DefaultFactory() { }
  static DefaultFactory instance;
 
  public static AbstractStrategyFactory getInstance() {
    if (instance == null)
      instance = new DefaultFactory();
    return instance;
  }
  public MessageStrategy createStrategy(final MessageBody mb) {
    return new MessageStrategy() {
      MessageBody body = mb;
      public void sendMessage() {
        Object obj = body.getPayload();
        System.out.println((String) obj);
      }
    };
  }
}

The joke slide, right after green: this is what “I will probably need this functionality soon” looks like. Don’t read the code; point at it and let the room read “Hello World!” in the middle of it.

10–20 seconds. What is written down, first on the test list and then as tests, no longer has to be held in your head: less to keep track of, more room to focus on the problem, and the examples end up as executable documentation.

12 minutes of TDD with a hard stop at a checkpoint tag. Plant three things on the test list: “Josh wins x to y” (ask the room what x is: sets up GLM), “A beats K” (sets up the 2016 run), and one Obvious Implementation (sets up probity forbidding it). The old days

The evidence for humans

40–90%

fewer defects in 4 teams at Microsoft and IBM (Nagappan 2008)

15–35%

more development time (the teams’ own estimate)

→ Fucci 2017: steady, short cycles mattered more than test-first

→ Ghafari 2020: studies disagree mostly because their setups differ

Built around human limitations. Which ones does an agent have?

About 75 seconds. “So does it work? The best industrial data we have is Microsoft and IBM: four teams, 40 to 90 percent lower defect density, for 15 to 35 percent more time, by their own estimate. You pay up front. In my experience, that’s what buys a predictable pace: you spend less time firefighting later, and you can ship with confidence. But the research is messy. Many studies use students on toy problems, and they disagree mostly because they’re set up differently. When one study pulled the factors apart, the short, steady rhythm mattered more than writing the test first. And honestly: who would pay to build the same software twice, with equally good teams? Nobody. Until now. With agents, I ran the same kata ten times, for a few dollars each. So here’s the question: TDD is built around human limitations. Which ones does an agent have?” Precise if asked: the defect figure is pre-release defect density, and the time figure is the teams’ own estimate. Don’t claim modular design here: these studies didn’t measure it, and part 2 shows the agents’ design didn’t change.

Part 2

The new ways

What happened when agents were told to do TDD

21:00–36:00.

The new ways · An agent ≠ a human

Which of TDD’s benefits does an agent need?

It doesn’t have

Fear

Boredom

Context switching fatigue

Not knowing where the code is going

Just like us, or worse

Misreading the spec

Claiming done when it isn’t

Blind spots in its own tests

Gold plating

Discipline inconsistency

In my experiment, one agent put the same misreading in its test and its code.

Callback to “which ones does an agent have?”. Discipline inconsistency is one we share: the seb branch labelled commits RED that never failed, Opus wrote code ahead of its tests, and probity had to block 13 writes to keep its run on track. Beck watches his own agent for unrequested features. Gold plating is the human benefit that partly carries over: probity rejected two greens that went too far. Be fair: no run gold-plated this kata (14–32 lines of production code each).

The new ways

What others found

Birgitta Böckeler · Aug 2026

TDD prompts gave no quality gain, for 3–8.5× the tokens.

Emily Bache · Sep 2026

That tested a prompt, not TDD. Missing: a test list and a harness.

→ So I tested both: a TDD prompt and a TDD harness.

Böckeler: “TDD inside the agent loop: theater or actual value?”, martinfowler.com, 10 Aug 2026. Bache: response video on Modern Software Engineering, 23 Sep 2026. Both are summaries, not quotes. Say what a harness means here: tooling that blocks the agent until a rule passes, not the coding agent itself.

Introduce the cast once, so the names later on make sense. Opus, DeepSeek, GLM, Qwen and Gemma are models; Astra’s plan was agreed with me before it wrote any code; the unrecorded agent is the seb branch from March. The no-TDD run is the baseline (blue row); my 2016 run is the human one. Say it before anyone asks: n = 1 per setup, on a 20-line kata the models have seen many times. Two runs of the same model differed more (8 of 9 vs 5 of 9 planted bugs caught) than the process changed anything. Böckeler’s larger study shows the same pattern.

The new ways

Agents doing TDD: it looks good, but it’s a charade

46%

of new tests passed at once: the agent already knew the answer

→ GLM did TDD by the book, and still ships “Josh wins 1 to 2”

→ Ten implementations, one design: a rank string, indexOf, two counters

→ On this kata, TDD didn’t change the agents’ design. It only tidied it.

46% is 26 of 57 tests, across the six agents told to do TDD by prompt. GLM by the book: 7 of 7 genuine reds, every commit labelled correctly. GLM returns “Josh wins 1 to 2” when Josh wins 2–1, and its own tests say that is correct: ask the room again what x was. Callback to Laforgia’s quote from the myths slide: by his definition (tests as a tool to design code), design the tests didn’t change isn’t TDD. The evidence: the run without TDD has the same design. The tidying is composed method: the TDD runs’ refactor steps split the code into small functions (Opus: return formatResult(scoreRounds(steve, josh))), while the no-TDD run is one function. Be fair: that is a point in TDD’s favour. No agent injected anything.

The new ways

Tiny steps are less meaningful for an agent

Fake it

Increases cycle speed for humans. An agent doesn’t need this detour.

Minimal steps

Lower a human’s risk. An agent doesn’t need to play it this safe.

Gorman called it

The tests that drive the design aren’t always good regression tests

“A test first, not the tests”

Stops a human overinvesting. For an agent it’s cheap: GLM wrote all 7 tests first.

Callbacks to Gorman and Ottinger from the myths slide. If asked about minimal steps: they choose examples that are enough to drive the code, which is not the same as enough to protect it. Opus 5, the most minimal-step run, caught 5 of 9 planted bugs, but that is one run, so an observation, not a law. GLM on fake it: “TDD created a bug and then caught it”. GLM’s skipped tests: commit 0512a46, 7 skipped tests, 7 genuine reds. Beck’s reasons for one test at a time were human: rework, and the gloom of waiting for anything to pass.

The new ways

Enforcing TDD with a harness: probity

11 of 12

tests genuinely red

4

real refactors: the most faithful TDD in the repo

→ The same result as no TDD, at 13× the cost and 22× the time

→ It dropped tests that couldn’t go red, so it caught fewer bugs: 6 of 9, vs 7 without TDD

→ 9 of 13 blocks were wrong, and resending the edit usually worked

Callback to Bache: she said a harness was missing, so here it is. Probity 1.10.1 by Nizar Selander: a hook that blocks every production write unless an AI validator sees a failing test it addresses. It always enforces the smallest step, which is stricter than Beck’s TDD: callback to the Obvious Implementation planted in the demo. Bache was right that a harness improves adherence; it didn’t improve the result. One run, unattended, so Selander’s main claim (less hand-holding for an interactive human) went unmeasured.

The new ways

The cost: tokens, dollars and time

RunTimeCostPlanted bugs caught
No TDD · Opus 5.529 s$0.277 of 9
TDD by prompt · Opus 5, run 13 min 47 s$2.078 of 9
TDD by prompt · Opus 5, run 24 min 18 s$2.725 of 9
TDD enforced by probity · Opus 5.510 min 48 s$3.546 of 9

Small experiment: one run per setup, on an easy 20-line kata

8–13× the cost and 8–22× the time, with no measurable quality gain.

Measured from the session transcripts at list prices. Opus 5 costs $5/$25 per million tokens and Opus 5.5 $4/$20, so TDD by prompt on Opus 5.5 would be about a fifth cheaper. In absolute terms the money is trivial next to an hour of developer time; the point is that nothing measurable came back for it. Two runs of the same model caught 8 of 9 and 5 of 9. On bigger problems: more cycles, each resending a larger context, so the overhead grows (Opus: “It scales with the ceremony, not with the difficulty”). Fair caveat: on an unfamiliar problem the benefit may grow too, because the agent no longer knows the answer. On Jain’s much larger task the frontier model’s harness still cost about 7× for no quality gain.

The new ways · Naresh Jain, Oct 2026

Are harnesses worth the cost?

ModelHarnessAcceptedTimeCost
Sol (frontier)No10 of 106 min 51 s~$0.41
Sol (frontier)Yes10 of 1019 min 53 s~$2.68
Luna (cheap)No3 of 1015 min 56 s~$0.09
Luna (cheap)Yes10 of 1035 min~$0.27

→ His harness isn’t TDD: specs and examples to guide the agent, plus checks it runs itself

Frontier model: one independent check at the end. Cheap model: checks throughout.

“Are Harnesses Worth the Cost?”, martinfowler.com, 13 Oct 2026. A greenfield Java backend-for-frontend, 10 runs per arm. All four setups were judged by the same 178 external acceptance tests: that suite is the referee, not part of the harness. The harness took the cheap model from 3 of 10 to 10 of 10, and harnessed Luna still cost about a third less than unharnessed Sol. His recommendation matches this talk: for frontier models, run the independent check once as a final gate; for cheaper models, run it throughout.

Part 3

This is the way

For the coming year

36:00–42:00. A tribute to The Mandalorian: say it like Din Djarin. Seven slides in six minutes: keep moving. The buffer from dropping the herdr race covers the extra one.

This is the way · For the agent

What we keep, what we leave behind

Keep

✓ Examples agreed before any code

✓ A check the agent didn’t write

✓ A failing test first for every bug

✓ Refactoring on green

Leave behind

Fake it and minimal green

Forcing the smallest step

A perfect process as proof of quality

Red as the proof that a test can fail

→ Keep the proof, drop the ritual: mutation-test afterwards instead (Gorman, Böckeler)

For the agent, not for teaching humans: this is still how I teach people. Keep: the agreed examples and a check the agent didn’t write are the next slides. A failing test first for a bug is where red still carries information; that is outside this kata, but every agent agreed. Refactoring on green is what tidied the agents’ code. Leave behind: fake it guards against a human’s premature generalisation; the agent already knows the target, so it manufactures intermediate bugs. Beck’s own TDD allows bigger steps when you are confident (Obvious Implementation).

This is the way

Planning

Why? Less rework, and mutual understanding.

The ambiguity

GLM’s “Josh wins 1 to 2”: no agent’s TDD caught the “x to y” ambiguity.

One agreed example, “Josh wins 2 to 1”, would have caught it in seconds.

The expectations

Agreed with the team before the agent starts.

Astra agreed them with me first. Its suite is the only TDD one that pins down “x to y”.

The agent turns them into its own test list.

Lighter than spec-driven development (spec-kit, OpenSpec)

This talk was planned first

~70%

of the text is still the first draft, after every review round

Why planning matters to me: I give this talk, not the AI, and I can’t present what I can’t talk about. Part 1 comes from my own deck from 2013. Two lists that used to be one. The expectations (what must be true) are agreed with the team before the agent starts; Laforgia suggests writing them together, like a Specification by Example workshop. The test list (which unit tests, in what order) was the human’s working memory; it now belongs to the agent’s inner loop. Astra’s agreed plan also said “Read decks without modifying them”, but no test ever checked it: the gap that Expectation-Driven Development closes by making the agent prove each expectation. This talk as the example: we wrote and argued over the plan before generating any slides, and about 70% of the planned slides’ text (67.9%: 1,109 of 1,634 words) is still the first generated version. New requirements are left out: the three red/green/refactor slides imported from my old deck, the Expectation-Driven Development slide, the agenda and the references (with them included it is 54%). Measured per slide, so moving a slide is not a change, and deleted text doesn’t count either; images and code blocks are ignored. It was 86% when I first called the deck final; the review round after that brought it to 76%, and the plain-language pass and last fixes to about 70%. Measured 17 Oct 2026 with python3 presentation/deck/measure-changes.py --exclude step-red,step-green,step-refactor,edd,agenda,references.

This is the way

Vertical slicing

→ Small diffs a human can actually review

→ Fast incremental delivery at all layers

From experience, not from this experiment

“On anything non-trivial, the spec is never right. … Adapting to feedback is the real requirements discipline.”

Jason Gorman

UI

API

Domain

Data

One slice through every layer

Be explicit that this one comes from experience: the kata is a single slice, so the experiment says nothing about it. Gorman (LinkedIn, Oct 2026), the same Gorman as on the myths slide: you only find out the spec is wrong once real users see a working implementation. That is the answer to “isn’t spec-first just waterfall?”: plan, then slice small so the feedback comes fast.

This is the way

Move up a loop

Outer loop

The human

Inner loop

The agent

The double loop from Growing Object-Oriented Software (Freeman & Pryce, 2009)

→ Outer loop, agreed examples: the human

→ Inner loop, agent decides

“A human still owns what ships but now they’re reviewing evidence and not just diffs.”

Addy Osmani

Just BDD again? Yes. But the examples stay with you.

We are not abandoning TDD; we are moving up a loop. The old ideas that survive are the outer loop. Addy Osmani, “Agentic verification” (14 Oct 2026): writing code is no longer the bottleneck, verifying it is. In GOOS the outer loop starts with a failing acceptance test; for an agent, agreed examples are enough to start, and the agent makes them run. If someone says “that’s ATDD”: close, but ATDD writes the acceptance tests before the code. I only agree the examples; the agent makes them run and shows me the output.

This is the way

Specify behaviour with examples

This experiment

Only tests GLM and Gemma didn’t write caught their bugs

Mathews & Nagappan 2024

Tests given with the task help LLMs

Konstantinou et al. 2026

14% vs 25%

faults found by tests written after faulty code vs. independent tests

→ Jain: specs, examples and checks lifted a cheap model from 3 to 10 of 10

An example can be checked; a sentence can be misread.

The blue line in one story: the README’s “Josh wins x to y” was a sentence, and GLM and Gemma misread it; one example, “Josh wins 2 to 1”, would have settled it. GLM and Gemma had the same author for code and tests, so the same misreading sat in both; only a suite they didn’t write caught them (the acceptance suite, or any other agent’s winner-first suite). Mathews & Nagappan, “Test-Driven Development for Code Generation” (2024): supplying tests improves LLM success. Konstantinou, Tambon, Papadakis, “On the risk of coding before testing” (2026): tests generated after faulty code detect 14% of faults, against 25% for independently generated tests. Osmani: “Example tests say what should happen; properties say what must not.” Our hidden acceptance suite already did his differential testing: 1000 random games against a reference implementation.

This is the way · Andrea Laforgia, Mar 2026

Expectation-Driven Development

1

Write the expectations in plain text, before any code

2

The agent proves each one by running it, not by describing it

3

Critical paths become automated tests

“The fox can guard the henhouse if there’s a different fox checking the first fox’s work.”

Andrea Laforgia

His own caveat: not battle-tested yet

The same Laforgia as on the myths slide, three years on: his Substack post “Expectation-Driven Development” (21 March 2026) keeps TDD’s discipline of specifying behaviour before implementation, “without the ceremony”. Our data backs his two demands. Executed evidence, not narrated: one reflection was copied from another model, and one status log cites commit hashes that don’t exist. A different fox: only tests GLM and Gemma didn’t write themselves caught their bugs. His expectations start as plain sentences, and the previous slide says a sentence can be misread; that’s why each one has to be proven by running it. He says himself he hasn’t battle-tested it on a real project.

Test-first becomes example-first.

From Beck’s TDD by Example to Adzic’s Specification by Example.

Agree on BDD-style examples before any code.

Let the agent decide everything below them.

Have something the agent didn’t write check the result.

Questions?

Sebastian Larsson

42:00–44:00, then leave this slide up during Q&A: the takeaway stays on screen. The bookend: the old talk was called “TDD: By Example”. Three lines, three callbacks: the examples (Adzic), everything below them (move up a loop: the agent keeps its own test list and cycles), and something the agent didn’t write (Laforgia’s different fox; in the experiment, only tests GLM and Gemma didn’t write caught their bugs). Say it: this is my bet, not my measurement; no run tested the three lines together. If someone asks about BDD tools: the step definitions decide what actually gets checked, so they belong to the human or a second reviewer, not to the agent writing the code.
